memory_update.text: SPSC should be carried forward as the cleanest underfollowed retail-data/plumbing candidate for AI-mediated product discovery, especially around item data, fulfillment, inventory and supplier compliance workflows.
CRTO should be carried forward as the most direct small-cap retail-media platform candidate, but later layers must separate retail-media growth from legacy retargeting/ad-tech exposure.

YEXT should remain in the speculative shadow lane until evidence proves AI-search and structured-brand-data adoption is translating into retail/ecommerce revenue rather than generic marketing positioning.
The node appears to split into three investable sublayers: marketplace/retailer-owned demand surfaces, independent retail-media monetization platforms, and product/brand/availability data plumbing.

Many pure-play product information management, content syndication, reviews and digital shelf analytics leaders appear private or acquired, so public-market exposure may be indirect through broader commerce, ad-tech and retail supply-chain software names.

SPSC should be carried forward as the highest-fit underfollowed candidate for retail data plumbing: fulfillment compliance, catalog-aligned analytics, inventory/sales data, and trading-partner network effects.

CRTO should be carried forward as the retail-media and sponsored-product visibility candidate; key gate is whether commerce media growth is measurable and durable enough to offset legacy ad-tech risks.
RAMP should be tracked as a second-order retail-media clean-room and data-collaboration infrastructure candidate, not as direct product-content infrastructure.
YEXT is a speculative-shadow candidate for AI search/entity/discovery data; it needs proof of product-level ecommerce workflows before surviving later Serenity layers.

Pure public exposure to PIM, review syndication, digital shelf analytics, and marketplace content syndication appears limited; later passes should map private leaders and public acquirers/owners to avoid false purity assumptions.

For this node, the likely public-stock chokepoint may be less about AI model vendors and more about operational data rails: product catalog accuracy, retail trading rules, inventory availability, retail-media measurement, and permissioned brand-retailer data collaboration.

SPSC should be carried forward as the highest-quality underfollowed candidate for retail product-data and trading-partner infrastructure; next layer must prove AI-shopping relevance beyond generic supply-chain SaaS.
CRTO is a small-cap commerce-media/retail-media candidate with measurable retailer and brand network evidence, but must be separated from legacy retargeting and broader adtech cyclicality.
RAMP maps to retail media clean rooms and measurement rather than product content itself; carry as second-order data-collaboration exposure with regulatory and M&A status checks.

CMRC is the cleanest direct public mapping to product-feed and agentic catalog exports via Feedonomics, but its below-$300M market cap and business turnaround risks require speculative_shadow treatment.

Many best-fit product information management, review, syndication and marketplace optimization assets are private or acquired: Salsify, Syndigo, Bazaarvoice, PowerReviews, CommerceIQ, Rithum/ChannelAdvisor and Profitero. Public-market mapping is therefore imperfect and likely indirect.

For this node, strongest evidence gates are not AI mentions but measurable growth in product-feed/catalo​​g syndication, retailer onboarding, retail-media contribution, same-retailer retention, clean-room usage, catalog error reduction and inventory/content accuracy workflows.

SPSC is the strongest underfollowed candidate for the node because it maps directly to retailer-supplier product/item data validation, assortment, fulfillment, and inventory analytics rather than generic ecommerce software.

SMWB is a speculative small-cap digital shelf analytics candidate; inclusion depends on proving Retail Intelligence is material and tied to AI-mediated product discovery rather than just a product-label refresh.

YEXT is a speculative AI-search visibility and structured brand-data candidate; later layers should test whether Scout creates durable ARR reacceleration or remains a competitive feature in legacy local SEO/listings.

Retail-media measurement and data clean rooms are adjacent chokepoints to product discovery because retailer algorithms and AI agents need sales, audience, attribution, and product-level feedback loops.

Private companies dominate many pure-play product-content and digital-shelf categories, including ratings/reviews, PIM, marketplace optimization, and feed management; public-market exposure may be indirect or embedded in broader software/data companies.

node: AI-mediated shopping, retail data and product-content infrastructure
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expands the direct public-company universe for the node where consumer discovery shifts from human browsing and brand awareness toward machine-readable product facts, availability, retail-media bidding, ratings/reviews and marketplace ranking. The strongest direct exposures found in this pass are retail-media platforms and retail product-data networks rather than consumer brands themselves. Reference/context anchor: Instacart, because it owns grocery marketplace demand, retail-media inventory and closed-loop shopper data. Underfollowed lane: SPS Commerce, Criteo and Yext. SPS Commerce is the cleanest retail data/plumbing candidate; Criteo is the most direct independent retail-media monetization candidate; Yext is a smaller, more speculative AI-discovery structured-data candidate. This is not a buy/sell list; later layers must verify revenue sensitivity to AI shopping and retail-media adoption rather than generic ecommerce or ad-tech exposure. Layer 1B expanded the public-stock universe for the scarce-provider side of AI-mediated shopping and retail data infrastructure. The strongest public candidates are not pure PIM/digital-shelf vendors because many core vendors in product content, review syndication, and marketplace optimization appear private or embedded inside larger ad-tech/commerce stacks. The public chokepoint lane therefore clusters around retail trading-network data, commerce-media platforms, retail-media data collaboration, and AI-search/discovery data management. No investment recommendation is implied. Layer 1B expansion found a small set of US-listed
